newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. council renews W. Sahara mission for 4 months.
newsitem.headline: U.N. council renews W. Sahara mission for 4 months.

text.p: The Security Council unanimously approved on Thursday a four-month renewal, until September 30, of a U.N. mission sent to Western Sahara nearly six years ago to oversee a referendum on the future of the disputed territory.

The referendum was originally scheduled for January 1992 to decide whether the former Spanish colony should be incorporated into Morocco, which controls most of Western Sahara, or become independent, as demanded by the Polisario Front.

The referendum has been repeatedly postponed because of differences between the two sides over who should be eligible to vote in the phosphate-rich territory whose sparse population includes many nomads.

Renewal of the 230-member U.N. observer force, called the U.N. Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO), will allow time for another visit to the region by former U.S. Secretary of State James Baker, who was appointed in March to advise Secretary-General Kofi Annan how best to break the deadlock.

Baker, who made an exploratory trip last month as Annan's personal envoy, has the task of advising whether the original U.N. plan involving a referendum can still be implemented in its present form, whether adjustments acceptable to the two sides might be possible or whether other ways of resolving the conflict could be found.
A ceasefire that has largely held since September 1991 ended a brushfire war between Morocco and the Algerian-backed Polisario dating back to Spain's withdrawal from Western Sahara in 1976.
Baker is expected to make a return visit in June to Morocco, Algeria, Mauritania and the Polisario base at Tindouf, near Algeria's border with Morocco.
The council asked Annan to submit a comprehensive report by September 15 "on the results of his evaluation of all aspects of the Western Sahara issue."

Although MINURSO's mandate was renewed without any debate, American U.N. envoy Bill Richardson later issued a statement saying his government would not be able to support continuation of the U.N. mission in its present form unless there was significant progress by the parties.
"The Baker mission may very well constitute the last, best hope for resolution of the Western Sahara problem," he said.
"Absent significant progress by the parties toward a solution, the United States would not be able to continue to support MINURSO in its present form," Richardson added.
